title: Rahula awakens
hook: the Buddha teaches the six senses as not-self, and Rahula awakens

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nandaka teaching the nuns, and your line, the moon is full. Did you teach one thing kindly? Today the Buddha takes his own son into the forest. Day five hundred twelve.

We've met Rahula before in this collection: a boy taught with a mirror, then a young monk told to be like the earth and like water. Now, in the hundred and forty-seventh discourse, he's grown. One day near Savatthi, the Buddha reflects that the qualities that ripen into freedom have ripened in Rahula. So after the alms round he says: Rahula, bring your sitting cloth. We'll spend the day in the Dark Forest. A father and a son walk out of the city and sit down under a tree. The text adds that many thousands of gods followed them, wanting to hear. Today: Rahula awakens.
screen: `THE BOY WITH THE MIRROR, GROWN.` → `BRING YOUR SITTING CLOTH.` → `UNDER A TREE IN THE DARK FOREST.`

segments.voice: The teaching is a string of questions, and Rahula answers every one himself. Rahula, is the eye permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, venerable sir. And what is impermanent, is it suffering or ease? Suffering. And what is impermanent, suffering, bound to change: is it fit to be seen as, this is mine, this I am, this is my self? No, venerable sir. Then the same three questions again, for forms, the things the eye sees. For eye-consciousness, the seeing itself. For eye-contact, the meeting of eye and form. For the feeling, perception, choices and awareness that come out of that meeting. Then all of it over again, for the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind. Notice the method. The Buddha doesn't announce a doctrine and ask Rahula to accept it. He asks, and lets his son look and say what he sees. The Pali word under every answer is anicca: impermanent, changing. Not only the world out there, but the instrument doing the looking, and the looking itself. Then the conclusion. Seeing this, the Buddha says, a noble disciple grows disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with seeing, and becomes dispassionate, and through dispassion the mind is freed. While he was speaking, the text says, Rahula's mind was freed from the taints, through not clinging. And the gods who had followed saw something too: whatever has the nature to arise, all of that has the nature to cease. In the Vinaya's story of his going forth, the boy Rahula asks his father for his inheritance. Here, under a tree, he receives it, as questions.
screen: `IS THE EYE PERMANENT?` · `FORMS, SEEING, CONTACT, FEELING` · `SIX SENSES, THE SAME QUESTIONS` · `RAHULA'S MIND IS FREED` · then, large: `ALL OF IT CHANGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the senses. Keep your eyes open for a moment. Notice something you're seeing, and notice the seeing itself shifting: light, focus, a blink. Now close your eyes. A sound arrives and fades. A touch: the chair under you, air on your hands, changing even while you notice it. Each time something arises, you can say quietly, changing. Not as a sad word. Just as a true one. The bell holds the time.
Rahula awakens. Anicca, impermanence, seen in the senses themselves: the eye, what it sees, and the seeing. Today's word.
Your line: all of it changing. Today, when one sight or sound grabs you, notice that the eye and ear doing the grabbing are changing too. Day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers use this discourse's three questions as a pattern for insight practice: is it permanent, is it unsatisfactory, is it fit to be called self?

fork.setup: you're Rahula, under the tree. the Buddha asks: what is impermanent and bound to change, is it fit to be seen as 'this is my self'? what do you say?
options: yes, if it's my own eye.
only the mind is my self.
fork.reveal: Rahula answers no, every time, for every sense. the Buddha lets him see it for himself instead of telling him.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent, changing. Sanskrit anitya. here, the eye, what it sees, and the seeing itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rahula awakens means he woke up one morning enlightened.
what it means: his mind is freed from the taints while his father questions him about the six senses.
what a scholar hears: the same teaching appears in the Samyutta Nikaya's book on the six senses, and some readers see it as the ripening of years of training that began with the mirror talk in MN 61.
